TITLE: Glyphosate, steam and cutting for non‐native plant control in Alberta fescue grassland restoration
SPECIES: T1=Bromus inermis (B. inermis); T2=Agropyron cristatum (A. cristatum); T3=Centaurea maculosa (spotted knapweed); T4=Chrysanthemum leucanthemum (C. leucanthemum, ox-eye daisy); T5=Poa pratensis (P. pratensis); T6=Elymus repens (E. repens); T7=Lepidium densiflorum (common pepper weed); T8=Medicago lupulina (black medic); T9=Poa compressa (P. compressa); T10=Achillea millefolium (common yarrow); T11=Cirsium arvense; T12=Festuca campestris (rough fescue); T13=Selaginella densa (little club moss); T14=Verbascum thapsus (common mullein); T15=Verbena bracteata (prostrate vervain); T16=Bromus tectorum (B. tectorum); T17=Danthonia parryi; T18=Heterotheca villosa; T19=Phleum pratense
CONTEXT: We investigated simple, cost-effective, non-native plant management methods for multiple species in ecological restoration of grasslands in Alberta, Canada. The objective was to determine whether cutting, glyphosate application and steaming, without targeted species, could reduce or eliminate non-native grasses and forbs with low impact to the non-target native plant community. We hypothesized glyphosate would most effectively reduce non-native plant cover since it can move into roots; cutting would be least damaging to native species as it is similar to grazing defoliation; and steam would provide short-term kill of aboveground vegetation. Waterton Lakes National Park is located in the Rocky Mountains of southwest Alberta, forming an International Peace Park and United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) World Heritage Site with neighbouring Glacier National Park in Montana, USA. The foothills grasslands growing season is cool and wet in May and June then hot and dry in August and September. Mean 1990–2000 annual precipitation is 807.6 mm, with most occurring during winter; mean minimum and maximum temperatures are 1.3 and 10.6 °C, respectively (Environment Canada 2012). Research sites were within a 3-km radius, with abundant non-native annual and perennial species representing typical grassland disturbances that could not be addressed with unique management techniques due to time and cost constraints. Site 1 was a landfill for domestic waste between 1952 and 1999. Sites 2 and 3 were borrow pits for gravel quarries abandoned in the 1970s. Site 2 soil was sandy loam texture with mean pH 5.9 and C:N ratio 24. Site 3 soil was sand to sandy loam texture with mean pH 7.9 and C:N ratio 14. A randomized incomplete block design was used.
TEXT:
[1] (abs) Question: What are the effects of cutting, glyphosate application and steam application on abundance and diversity of non-native grasses and forbs and non-target native grasses and forbs in restoration of a complex disturbed fescue grassland?
[2] (abs) Location: Waterton Lakes National Park, Alberta, Canada.
[3] (abs) Methods: Cutting, glyphosate application and steam application treatments were implemented at three disturbed sites in an incomplete block design with a control.
[4] (abs) Plant communities were evaluated for four growing seasons, one before and three after management treatment implementation.
[5] (res) Results: Glyphosate reduced non-native grass cover for three growing seasons following application and non-native forbs for one growing season.
[6] (res) Glyphosate led to significant increases in non-native forb cover, more than double pre-existing values 2 and 3 yr after application.
[7] (res) Native species abundance and diversity were more negatively impacted by glyphosate on sites with higher abundance and diversity prior to management treatments.
[8] (res) Low frequency cutting over 2 yr did not consistently control non-native species, steam reduced non-native grass cover at the most heavily invaded site.
[9] (con) Conclusions: Site-specific conditions must be considered to develop effective control methods for non-native species.
[10] (con) No treatment effectively re-established native grassland communities.
[11] (con) Glyphosate application reduced non-native grasses, but not non-native forbs.
[12] (con) When native forbs were abundant prior to management, glyphosate reduced them.
[13] (con) Steam may have potential and should be further investigated.
[14] (con) This is one of only a few studies to investigate methods to manage multiple non-native species occurring with native species, rather than management of a single undesirable species, and is the first to assess steam as a management option for native grasslands.

[16] (res) Non-native grasses dominated Sites 1 and 2 and native forbs dominated Site 3.
[17] (res) Total species richness and diversity were highest at Site 3.
[18] (res) Non-native species abundance varied with site, with most species present at all sites pre-treatment.
[19] (res) Dominant species were Bromus inermis (mean: 7.5% cover in plots) and Elymus repens (L.) Gould (quack grass; 9.2%) at Site 1, B. inermis (9.0%) and Agropyron cristatum (3.5%) at Site 2, and Poa compressa L. (Canada blue grass; 3.3%) and A. cristatum (2.8%) at Site 3.
[20] (res) Cutting and steam had little significant impact on vegetation diversity and species richness.
[21] (res) They did not reduce non-native grass and forb cover relative to controls within a year, although over 3 yr, non-native grass cover was significantly lower with steam at Site 1 and with cutting at Site 3.
[22] (res) Glyphosate had significant impacts on vegetation in each year at each site.
[23] (res) Non-native grass cover was reduced with glyphosate.
[24] (res) Although only statistically significant at Site 1 in 2012, this was biologically significant in all years at all sites.
[25] (res) Non-native grass cover with glyphosate was 75% less than the control at Site 2 in 2012, and 50% at Site 1 and 84% at Site 2 in 2013.
[26] (res) Non-native grass species richness and diversity were significantly lower with glyphosate at Sites 1 and 2 in 2011 and at the end of the study relative to pre-treatment.
[27] (res) Native grass cover was <5% at all sites and did not significantly differ among treatments in any year.
[28] (res) Total diversity was significantly lower with glyphosate across sites in 2011 but only at Site 3 in 2012.
[29] (res) Prior to and immediately after treatment, non-native forb cover was <5% at all sites and treatments, except significantly lower with glyphosate at Site 1.
[30] (res) In 2012, non-native forb cover significantly increased with glyphosate at all sites, persisting in 2013 at two sites.
[31] (res) Non-native forb richness was significantly higher with glyphosate at Sites 1 and 2 in 2012 and 2013.
[32] (res) In 2011 and 2012 native forb cover and richness were significantly lower with glyphosate than controls at Site 3; but only cover at Site 2 in 2011 and Site 3 in 2013.
[33] (res) The native forb species Heterotheca villosa (Pursch) Shinners (hairy false golden aster) and Achillea millefolium L. (common yarrow) were eliminated by glyphosate.
[34] (res) Native forbs were least negatively impacted at Site 1 where pre-treatment cover was very low.
[35] (res) In 2013 the significantly higher native forb cover with glyphosate at Site 1 was due to increased Verbena bracteata Cav. ex Lag. & Rodr. (prostrate vervain), only found at this site.
[36] (res) By the end of the study non-native forb cover was significantly higher with glyphosate than pre-treatment at Sites 1 and 2, and native forb cover had significantly decreased with glyphosate at Site 3 (Figs 1 and 2).
[37] (res) Flowering and seed set of non-native grasses was significantly reduced with glyphosate at Site 1, and that of nonnative forbs was significantly reduced with cutting and glyphosate at Site 2.
[38] (res) At Site 3, treatment had no effect on non-native plant flowering and seed production, although it significantly reduced that of native grasses and forbs.
[39] (res) Individual non-native plant species had variable responses to treatments, with high variability within a site.
[40] (res) Cutting and steam had no effect on any species.
[41] (res) Within sites, A. cristatum (Site 1), Poa pratensis L. (Kentucky blue grass) and P. compressa (Site 2) were significantly reduced with glyphosate.
[42] (res) P. pratensis and E. repens were eliminated from Site 3.
[43] (res) Treatment effects on individual species were most significant in 2011, mainly between glyphosate and the control.
[44] (res) P. compressa at all sites, and B. inermis and P. pratensis at Site 2, were significantly reduced with glyphosate relative to the control and most other treatments.
[45] (res) By 2013, there were no significant treatment effects on these species, suggesting non-native grasses had recovered.

[47] (res) Non-native (a,b) and native (c,d) mean vegetation cover at three restoration sites prior to (2010) and following (2011 to 2013) treatments to manage non-native plants.
[48] (res) Treatments are control (black), cut (white), glyphosate (grey) and steam (hash).
[49] (res) Bars represent $\pm$ 2 standard error.
[50] (res) Columns within years that do not share a common letter are significantly different.
[51] (res) At all sites, non-native forbs significantly increased with glyphosate in 2012, and remained significantly higher in 2013 at two sites.
[52] (res) Increased cover was mainly due to Lepidium densiflorum Scrad. (common pepper weed) and Medicago lupulina L. [57] (res) Site conditions explained the larger impact of glyphosate on native plant species at Sites 2 and 3.
